title: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Four head states suffice for random-looking Turing machine behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Two-color Turing machines with four head states can produce seemingly random behavior (about five in every million such rules), and allowing more than four states makes apparent randomness only slightly more common without changing the kinds of behavior seen.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: With four states, however, more complicated behavior immediately becomes possible. Indeed, in about five out of every million rules of this kind, one gets patterns with features that seem in many respects random

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “Turing Machines” (from p. 78), p. 79. Scope: two-color Turing machines with four or more head states, blank initial tape

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The existence of four-state random-looking examples and an approximate rate can be tested with current computation. The assertion over every larger state count and unchanged behavior taxonomy cannot be exhaustively covered.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample or enumerate four-state and larger two-color machines from blank tape, apply fixed randomness statistics to their spacetime outputs, and estimate qualifying frequencies with confidence intervals. Compare discovered behavior classes and rates across state counts.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The four-state rule space and larger spaces grow rapidly.

More than four states has no upper bound.

Seemingly random depends on test choices and runtime.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.75
data adequacy: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The numerical claim is a rate, about five per million, in a completely defined ensemble of four-state two-color machines. Sampling millions of short blank-tape runs estimates that rate to within the slack of the word 'about,' and the same sample design compares five or more states. A full enumeration is unnecessary for a rate, and the classifier has to be frozen in advance.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Sample two-color Turing machines with four or more head states on a blank tape, apply a fixed randomness classifier, and estimate the hit rate. The claim is confirmed if four-state rules yield on the order of five random-looking patterns per million and additional states raise that rate only slightly, and refuted if the rate is far from that or jumps sharply with more states.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The four-state space has about four billion rules, so the rate is estimated by sampling rather than by a full census.

Seemingly random is classifier-dependent, and the same classifier must be used at every state count.

fields.value:
